issues.item: Victim Similarity: People who look similar to the victims
issues.explanation: For a 57-year-old male with a life-threatening accident, 'people who look similar to the victims' is hard to reconcile unless multiple identifiable victims were involved; this reads more like an interpersonal/assault or disaster context than a typical accident-based trigger profile.

issues.item: Exposed to Others: I feel that others can see what happened to me just by looking at me
issues.explanation: 'I feel that others can see what happened to me just by looking at me' implies shame/visible mark/social exposure concerns that are not supported by the rest of the selected profile. With no memory, threat, or strategy items linking to visible injury or interpersonal scrutiny, this appraisal does not fit coherently with the accident-focused triggers.

issues.item: Triggers: Loss of Control: Lack of control
issues.explanation: The profile is not clinically coherent because the formulation specifies no active edges between nodes, implying the selected nodes should not form a tightly linked PTSD pattern. However, the trigger 'Lack of control' and the appraisal 'I can no longer trust my own body' are naturally connected in a life-threatening accident presentation, and the appraisal set itself forms a strong post-traumatic meaning cluster rather than isolated components.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Lost Meaning: Nothing in my life feels meaningful anymore
issues.explanation: Within the Negative Appraisals node, the items are not contradictory, but they cluster around severe global defeat/disconnection ('Nothing in my life feels meaningful anymore', 'I feel dead inside') plus somatic mistrust after accident trauma ('I can no longer trust my own body'). This is clinically plausible on its own, but together with the trigger content it implies an integrated trauma formulation that conflicts with the fully disconnected edge structure.

issues.item: Triggers: Tactile (Temperature): A specific temperature on the skin
issues.explanation: The profile is clinically incoherent because the cognitive formulation specifies no active edges at all, yet the selected Triggers and Negative Appraisals imply a linked trauma network. Concrete accident reminders (car sounds, crash imagery, temperature on skin) would ordinarily connect to threat, memory, or appraisals; presenting them alongside strong post-traumatic self-appraisals without any connecting nodes is inconsistent with the formulation structure.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Emotional Numbness: I feel dead inside
issues.explanation: Within the available nodes, the Negative Appraisals are internally coherent, and the Triggers are broadly plausible for a life-threatening accident. The main problem is cross-node/formulation mismatch: specific sensory accident triggers and severe trauma-related appraisals are both present, but the formulation says these components are not linked to each other or to any other PTSD processes.

vignette:
Mark is a 57-year-old interior designer who came to treatment more than a year after a life-threatening car accident that he still describes as if it is happening in front of him. At the time of the crash, he had been driving home from a client meeting, tired but alert, moving through a busy intersection on a familiar route. Another car struck the side of his vehicle with enough force to spin it. He remembers the violent sideways impact, the burst of sound from crumpling metal and brakes, and the helpless, suspended second in which he understood that he could not stop what was happening. What remains most vivid to him is not a full, orderly memory but the visual image of damaged cars locked together at odd angles and the noise around them—engines, tires, horns, voices he could not make sense of. He survived, but the experience left him with a sense that his body had failed him at the exact moment he most needed it to keep him safe.

In the weeks afterward, Mark found that ordinary parts of daily life had begun to take on the quality of warning signals. If he passed a roadside collision, even a minor one, he felt seized by the same mental picture of smashed vehicles and the same sick certainty that catastrophe could arrive without notice. Car sounds were especially difficult. The abrupt squeal of brakes outside his apartment, a horn in traffic, the low grind of engines idling near a loading zone could stop him mid-thought and pull his attention away from whatever he was doing. As an interior designer, much of his work depends on traveling to clients’ homes, meeting contractors, and visiting showrooms around the city. He began noticing how often his workday placed him near traffic: waiting for rides in front of buildings, standing beside busy streets with fabric samples in hand, hearing vehicles outside a consultation. He did not describe these moments as simple reminders. To him, they felt charged, as if the accident were close by and could break through again.

Conversations became difficult in a similar way. When clients, coworkers, or friends mentioned a wreck on the highway or a family member’s fender bender, Mark’s attention narrowed immediately. He would go quiet or change the subject abruptly, later feeling embarrassed by how visibly unsettled he had become. Over time he started steering conversations away from roads, travel, and local news, and he declined some social invitations if he thought the evening would involve long drives or casual talk about recent events in town. His world grew smaller in ways that were practical enough to seem reasonable to him at first. He told himself he was being careful, that there was no point putting himself in situations that would set him off in the middle of a client meeting. But the accumulation of these choices altered his work. He scheduled fewer in-person visits, leaned more heavily on email and remote consultations, and noticed a distance developing with clients who had once relied on his ease and presence.

Running alongside this was a painful shift in how he thought about himself. Mark had come to believe that he could no longer trust his own body. The fact that he had been alive and functioning normally one moment and trapped in violent impact the next felt, to him, like proof that his body was unreliable and fundamentally vulnerable. He paid close attention to physical sensations and interpreted them bleakly: tension, fatigue, or a surge of adrenaline did not feel temporary but like evidence that something in him had been permanently altered. He said more than once that he did not know himself anymore. Before the accident he thought of himself as composed, aesthetically driven, and capable of moving through complicated environments with confidence. Now he experienced himself as wary, easily shaken, and diminished. What frightened him most was the conviction that this was not a phase but a lasting reduction of who he was. He was certain that he had changed for the worse.

By the time he sought help, these beliefs had settled into the texture of everyday life. A recent incident finally pushed him to call: while on his way to a design installation, he saw two damaged cars pulled to the shoulder and was flooded with the old crash image so intensely that he had to stop what he was doing and step away before meeting the client. He later felt humiliated and deeply discouraged. In session, he spoke less about wanting to “get over” the accident than about wanting to understand whether any version of himself was still intact. He was afraid that the man he had been before the crash was gone for good, and he was hoping, cautiously, that treatment might help him live in a world of cars, sounds, and ordinary conversation without feeling that disaster was constantly about to return.
